cse-1993-ii-b-9.approach: A half adder gives $S=x\oplus y$ and $C=xy$. Tie one input to logic 1 and the sum output becomes NOT; the carry output is AND. Since $\{\text{AND},\text{NOT}\}$ is functionally complete, half adders alone realise any Boolean function.

steps.title: Outputs of one half adder
steps.body: For inputs $x,y$: $$S=x\oplus y,\qquad C=x\cdot y$$ So the carry output is already a 2-input **AND** gate.

steps.title: NOT from the sum output
steps.body: Fix $y=1$: $$S=x\oplus 1=\overline{x}$$ (if $x=0$, $S=1$; if $x=1$, $S=0$). So the sum output of a half adder with one input tied to 1 is an **inverter**.

steps.title: OR also follows
steps.body: By De Morgan, $x+y=\overline{\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}}$: two half adders as inverters, one as AND (carry), one more as inverter. (Also $x+y=(x\oplus y)\oplus(xy)$ using one half adder's $S$ and $C$ fed into a second half adder's inputs: its sum output is $x\oplus y\oplus xy=x+y$.)

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: AND and NOT (hence also OR) can be built only from half adders. Every Boolean function has a sum-of-products form using only AND, OR, NOT, so **every Boolean function can be implemented with half adders alone**.

answer.value: Carry $=xy$ gives AND; sum with one input tied to 1 gives $x\oplus1=\overline{x}$ (NOT). $\{\text{AND},\text{NOT}\}$ is functionally complete, so any Boolean function can be built from half adders.

pitfalls: Forgetting that a constant 1 input is allowed — without it, XOR and AND alone cannot produce NOT (they map all-zero inputs to 0).
cse-1993-ii-b-9.verification: Checked $x\oplus1$ on both values of $x$, and $(x\oplus y)\oplus xy$ on all four input pairs: 0,1,1,1 = OR.

cse-1993-ii-b-10.approach: Mode 2 is autoincrement register-indirect with RegR = PC. After fetching the one-word instruction at 2000 the PC already holds 2001, so the operand is taken from 2001 and the autoincrement then moves PC to 2002.

steps.title: PC after instruction fetch
steps.body: The instruction occupies one word at address 2000. During fetch the PC is incremented: $$PC = 2000+1 = 2001$$

steps.title: Operand address
steps.body: Mode 2: RegR (here PC) contains the address of the operand, so the operand address $= PC = \mathbf{2001}$. (This is effectively an immediate operand stored in the word after the instruction.)

steps.title: PC after execution
steps.body: After fetching the operand, RegR is incremented by 1: $$PC = 2001+1=\mathbf{2002}$$ Being a non-jump instruction, nothing else changes PC, so the next instruction is fetched from 2002.

pitfalls: Taking the operand address as 2000 — the PC was already incremented by the instruction fetch.
Answering 2001 for (b) and forgetting the mode-2 post-increment.
cse-1993-ii-b-10.verification: Memory layout: 2000 = instruction, 2001 = operand (consumed via PC), 2002 = next instruction — consistent with a 2-word immediate instruction.

cse-1993-ii-b-11.approach: A word is always read from $M_1$. A request that refers to $M_2$ first costs a page transfer $T_1$ into $M_1$; a request that refers to $M_3$ costs $T_2$ (into $M_2$) and $T_1$ (into $M_1$). Weight each case by its probability.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: $$t_A = p_1t_1 + p_2(T_1+t_1) + p_3(T_2+T_1+t_1)$$ A hit in $M_1$ costs $t_1$; a reference to $M_2$ means a page swap $M_2\to M_1$ ($T_1$) and then the read from $M_1$; a reference to $M_3$ needs $M_3\to M_2$ ($T_2$) and $M_2\to M_1$ ($T_1$) first.

answer.value: $t_A\approx 1.3\times10^{-5}$ s (13 µs)

pitfalls: Using only $\sum p_it_i$ (≈ 1.1 µs) — this ignores the page-transfer times, which dominate.
The transfer times are in seconds while access times are microseconds — keep the units consistent.
cse-1993-ii-b-11.verification: Alternative model reading the word at the level where it lives, $p_1t_1+p_2(t_2+T_1)+p_3(t_3+T_2+T_1)$, gives $0.99+10.08+2.02\approx13.09\,\mu s$ — also $\approx1.3\times10^{-5}$ s, so the result is robust; the exact 13.000 µs suggests the first model is the intended one.

cse-1993-ii-b-12.approach: Treat the single loop as a row-major walk over the $n\times n$ array: advance $j$ along a row, and at the last column reset $j$ and move to the next row; stop when $i$ runs past the last row.

steps.title: [A]: initial max
steps.body: max must start at an actual array element (any initial constant could be larger than every element). Start at the first cell: **[A] = A[0,0]**.

scene.code:
max := A[0,0]; i := 0; j := 0;
while i < n do
begin
  if A[i,j] > max then max := A[i,j];
  if j < n-1 then j := j+1
  else begin j := 0; i := i+1 end
end

steps.title: [C], [D]: moving to the next cell
steps.body: Within a row, $j$ goes $0,1,\dots,n-1$. While $j<n-1$ we can still step right: **[C] = j < n-1**. At $j=n-1$ the else-branch sets $j:=0$ and must go to the next row: **[D] = i+1**.

steps.title: [B]: loop condition
steps.body: Rows are $0\dots n-1$. After the last cell $(n-1,n-1)$ the else-branch makes $i=n$, so loop while **[B] = i < n** (equivalently $i\le n-1$).

steps.title: Check on n = 2
steps.body: Cells visited: $(0,0)\to(0,1)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)\to$ then $j=0,i=2$ and the loop stops. All $n^2=4$ cells are compared exactly once.

pitfalls: Initialising max to 0 fails when all elements are negative.
Using [C] = j < n would let j reach n — out of bounds.
cse-1993-ii-b-12.verification: Traced n = 1 (one comparison, then i = 1 ends the loop) and n = 2 (four cells in row-major order).

cse-1993-ii-b-13.approach: Without a header (or a pointer to the predecessor) we cannot link a node before X. Instead insert Y after X and swap the data of X and Y — the classic O(1) 'insert before' trick.

steps.title: Intended result
steps.body: The printed target omits $d$; the intended list is $d_1,\dots,d_{j-1},\,d,\,d_j,\dots,d_n$ — i.e. insert $d$ **before** the node X holding $d_j$. Its predecessor is not reachable from X.

steps.title: Splice Y after X
Swap the data
steps.body:
```
temp = X->data;
X->data = Y->data;   /* X now holds d  */
Y->data = temp;      /* Y now holds dj */
```
Result: $d_1,\dots,d_{j-1},d,d_j,d_{j+1},\dots,d_n$ — done in $O(1)$ without any header or traversal.

scene.caption: data of X and Y swapped

steps.title: Edge case j = n
steps.body: If X is the last node, $X\to next$ is NULL; the same code works (Y becomes last, holding $d_n$).

answer.value: Y→next := X→next; X→next := Y; swap(X→data, Y→data). Gives $d_1,\dots,d_{j-1},d,d_j,\dots,d_n$ in O(1).

pitfalls: Setting X->next = Y before saving X->next loses the rest of the list.
Trying to find the predecessor — impossible without the head pointer.
cse-1993-ii-b-13.verification: Checked j = 1 (new data becomes first item) and j = n (old last item moves into Y, which becomes the tail).

cse-1993-ii-b-14.approach: Count records per block for the data area, then build the index bottom-up: one (key, block-pointer) entry per block of the level below, until a level fits in a single block.

steps.title: Data area
steps.body: Records per block $=512/64=8$. Records $=16\text{K}=16384$. $$\text{data blocks}=16384/8=\mathbf{2048}$$

steps.title: Index entry size
steps.body: Entry = key + block address $=14+2=16$ bytes, so index blocking factor $=512/16=32$ entries per block.

steps.title: Index levels
steps.body:
Level 1: one entry per data block → $2048/32=64$ blocks.

Level 2: one entry per level-1 block → $\lceil 64/32ceil=2$ blocks.

Level 3: $\lceil 2/32ceil = 1$ block (root).

Index area $=64+2+1=\mathbf{67}$ blocks in **3 levels**.

answer.value: Data area = 2048 blocks; index area = 64 + 2 + 1 = 67 blocks; 3 index levels

pitfalls: Indexing every record (16384 entries) instead of every data block — ISAM's index is sparse.
Forgetting the 2-byte pointer in the index entry size.

cse-1993-ii-b-15.approach: Each call runs its for-loop $n-1$ times (one if-test per pass) and then recurses on $n-1$; unroll the recurrence.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: With argument $n$ the loop executes the if-statement for $i=1,\dots,n-1$, i.e. $n-1$ times, then calls bubblesort$(n-1)$: $$a_n=a_{n-1}+(n-1),\qquad a_1=0$$ (for $n=1$ the loop `for i:=1 to 0` runs zero times; the code has no explicit base case, so we take the recursion to stop there.)

pitfalls: Writing $a_n=a_{n-1}+n$ — the loop runs to $n-1$.
The comparison count is independent of the input order (no early exit).

cse-1993-ii-b-16.approach: Induct on the number of non-leaf (internal) nodes $I$, showing leaves $L=I+1$. Replacing a leaf by an internal node with two leaf children adds one internal node and one net leaf.

steps.title: Statement and base
steps.body: Claim: every binary tree in which each non-leaf has exactly 2 children satisfies $L=I+1$.\n\nBase $I=0$: the tree is a single node, which is a leaf: $L=1=0+1$. ✓

steps.title: Inductive hypothesis
steps.body: Assume $L=I+1$ for every such tree with $k\ge0$ internal nodes.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body: Take a tree $T$ with $k+1$ internal nodes. Some internal node $v$ has two leaf children (pick a deepest internal node). Delete both children: $v$ becomes a leaf, giving a full tree $T'$ with $I'=k$ internal nodes and $L'=L-2+1=L-1$ leaves. By hypothesis $L'=k+1$, so $$L=L'+1=k+2=(k+1)+1=I+1.$$ ✓

scene.caption: remove the two leaf children of v: I drops by 1, L drops by 1

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: By induction, in every binary tree where each non-leaf node has 2 descendants, the number of leaves is one more than the number of non-leaf nodes.

answer.value: Induction on internal nodes $I$: base $I=0\Rightarrow L=1$; removing the two leaf children of a deepest internal node reduces both $I$ and $L$ by 1, so $L=I+1$ holds for all such trees.

pitfalls: Inducting on total nodes without showing that a node with two leaf children exists.
The result fails for trees where some node has only one child.
cse-1993-ii-b-16.verification: Root with two leaves: $I=1,L=2$. Complete tree of height 2: $I=3,L=4$.

cse-1993-ii-b-17.approach: Use a Venn diagram with unknown exactly-two regions $x,y,z$. Inclusion–exclusion shows the data are inconsistent if everyone eats something, and otherwise only bound the answer between 5 and 10.

steps.title: Regions
steps.body: Let $x=$ exactly V,F; $y=$ exactly V,E; $z=$ exactly F,E (all $\ge0$). Then only-V $=9-5-x-y=4-x-y$, only-F $=10-5-x-z=5-x-z$, only-E $=7-5-y-z=2-y-z$; all must be $\ge0$.

steps.title: If everyone eats a dish
steps.body: $|V\cup F\cup E|=21$ would need $$21=(9+10+7)-(5+x+5+y+5+z)+5=16-(x+y+z)$$ i.e. $x+y+z=-5<0$: **impossible**. The data cannot be consistent if all 21 eat at least one dish; at most 16 persons eat anything.

steps.title: At least two dishes
steps.body: At least two $=x+y+z+5$. From $x+y\le4$, $x+z\le5$, $y+z\le2$: $2(x+y+z)\le11\Rightarrow x+y+z\le5$ (attained by $x=4,z=1,y=0$). Minimum is $x=y=z=0$. Hence $$5\le\text{at least two}\le10$$ and the value is **not uniquely determined**.

steps.title: Takeaway
steps.body: At least the 5 who eat all three eat two or more, so the stored answer 3 is impossible. With the most natural extra assumption (nobody eats exactly two dishes) the answer is **5**, and then $21-11=10$ persons eat none.

answer.value: Not uniquely determined: at least two dishes is between 5 and 10 (it is ≥ 5 because 5 eat all three). If no one eats exactly two, the answer is 5. The data are inconsistent if every person eats at least one dish.
answer.keyNote: The committed key '3' is impossible: the 5 people who eat all three dishes already eat at least two. The printed data do not fix a unique value; corrected and flagged for review.

pitfalls: Assuming all 21 eat at least one dish — it leads to a negative region count.
Answering below 5 ignores the 5 who eat all three.
cse-1993-ii-b-17.verification: Example $x=4,y=0,z=1$: regions only-V 0, only-F 0, only-E 1, union $=16-5=11$; at least two $=10$. Example $x=y=z=0$: union 16, at least two 5. Both satisfy every given count.

cse-1993-ii-b-18.approach: C is a logical consequence of $F$ iff every row where $F$ is true also has $C$ true. Build the 8-row truth table of $F=A\wedge(A\to(B\vee C))\wedge(B\to\sim A)$.

steps.title: Truth table
steps.body: $F$ is a conjunction, so it needs $A=1$; then $B\to\sim A$ forces $B=0$; then $A\to(B\vee C)$ forces $C=1$.

steps.title: Rows where F is true
steps.body: Only the row $A=1,B=0,C=1$ gives $F=1$: $1\wedge(1\to(0\vee1))\wedge(0\to0)=1\wedge1\wedge1=1$. In that row $C=1$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Every row with $F=1$ has $C=1$, so $F\to C$ is a tautology and $C$ is a logical consequence of $F$.

answer.value: F is true only for A = 1, B = 0, C = 1, where C is true; hence $F\Rightarrow C$ (C is a logical consequence).

pitfalls: Checking only that F and C can be simultaneously true — consequence needs C true in **every** model of F.
cse-1993-ii-b-18.verification: Resolution check: from A and B→¬A get ¬B; from A and A→(B∨C) get B∨C; with ¬B, C.

cse-1993-ii-c-19.approach: A two-level NAND–NAND network is a sum of products. Read the product terms off the first-level gates to get $D_A$ and $D_B$; for D flip-flops $A^+=D_A$, $B^+=D_B$, then tabulate all 8 combinations of $A,B,P$.

steps.title: Read the circuit
steps.body: First-level gate inputs: $(\overline{A},B)$ and $(\overline{A},\overline{P})$ feed the $D_A$ gate; $(P,\overline{B})$ and $(\overline{P},A)$ feed the $D_B$ gate.

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body: $$D_A=\overline{\overline{\overline{A}B}\cdot\overline{\overline{A}\,\overline{P}}}=\overline{A}B+\overline{A}\,\overline{P}=\overline{A}(B+\overline{P})$$ $$D_B=\overline{\overline{P\overline{B}}\cdot\overline{\overline{P}A}}=P\overline{B}+\overline{P}A$$ With D flip-flops, $A^+=D_A$ and $B^+=D_B$.

answer.value: $D_A=\overline{A}B+\overline{A}\,\overline{P}$, $D_B=P\overline{B}+\overline{P}A$. AB → A⁺B⁺ for P = 0 / P = 1: 00 → 10 / 01; 01 → 10 / 10; 10 → 01 / 01; 11 → 01 / 00.

pitfalls: Treating the gates as AND–OR without the double inversion — NAND–NAND equals AND–OR, not NOR.
Mixing up which feedback line is $A$ and which is $\overline{A}$.

cse-1993-ii-c-20.approach: Trace the loop: HL is a pointer loaded indirectly from 5000H, B is a down-counter of 5, and each iteration reads input port 20H into A and stores it at the pointer.

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body: `LHLD 5000` loads L from 5000H and H from 5001H, so HL = the 16-bit address stored at 5000H–5001H (a pointer to a buffer). `MVI B,5` sets the loop counter to 5.

scene.code:
LHLD 5000   ; L <- [5000H], H <- [5001H]
      MVI  B, 5   ; counter = 5
GET:  IN   20     ; A <- port 20H
      MOV  M, A   ; [HL] <- A
      INX  H      ; HL <- HL + 1
      DCR  B      ; B <- B - 1, sets Z
      JNZ  GET    ; repeat while B != 0

steps.title: Loop body
steps.body: `IN 20` reads a byte from input port 20H into A; `MOV M,A` stores it at the address in HL; `INX H` advances the pointer; `DCR B` decrements the counter and sets Z; `JNZ GET` repeats until B = 0.

steps.title: Function and roles
steps.body: **(a)** Reads **5 bytes** from input port **20H** and stores them in **5 consecutive memory locations** starting at the address held in 5000H/5001H.\n\n**(b)** A: receives the input byte; H,L: memory pointer (destination address, incremented); B: byte counter (5 → 0); flags: Z from DCR ends the loop. Addresses: 5000H/5001H (pointer), port 20H (input device), and the 5-byte buffer pointed to by HL.

answer.value: Inputs 5 bytes from port 20H into consecutive memory locations starting at the address stored at 5000H (low) / 5001H (high). A = data byte, HL = memory pointer, B = counter, Z flag terminates the loop.

pitfalls: Reading LHLD 5000 as HL ← 5000H — LHLD loads HL from memory 5000H/5001H (direct addressing).
INX H does not affect flags; the Z flag comes from DCR B.
cse-1993-ii-c-20.verification: B takes values 5,4,3,2,1 at IN — five reads; after the fifth DCR, B = 0 and JNZ falls through.

cse-1993-ii-c-21.approach: Simulate both policies with 4 frames, starting empty. LRU evicts the page whose last use is oldest; FIFO evicts the page loaded earliest.

steps.title: LRU: cold start
steps.body: References 1–4 (pages 1,2,3,4) fault and fill the 4 frames. Pages 1 and 3 (refs 5,6) hit.

steps.title: LRU: replacements
steps.body: Ref 7 (page 5): last uses 1@5, 2@2, 3@6, 4@4 → evict 2. Ref 8 (page 2): evict 4 (last used @4). Refs 9, 10 (1, 5) hit. Ref 11 (page 4): last uses 1@9, 3@6, 5@10, 2@8 → evict 3. Ref 12 (page 3): evict 2 (@8). Ref 13 (page 2): evict 1 (@9). Ref 14 (page 3) hits.

steps.title: FIFO
steps.body: Load order 1,2,3,4. Refs 5,6 hit. Ref 7 (5): evict 1 → queue 2,3,4,5. Ref 8 (2) hit. Ref 9 (1): evict 2 → 3,4,5,1. Refs 10–12 (5,4,3) hit. Ref 13 (2): evict 3 → 4,5,1,2. Ref 14 (3): evict 4 → 5,1,2,3.

steps.title: FIFO result
steps.body: Faults at references **1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 13, 14** (pages 1,2,3,4,5,1,2,3) — **8 faults**. Here FIFO happens to beat LRU.

answer.value: (a) LRU: faults at references 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13 (pages 1,2,3,4,5,2,4,3,2) — 9 faults. (b) FIFO: faults at references 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 13, 14 (pages 1,2,3,4,5,1,2,3) — 8 faults.

pitfalls: In FIFO a hit does not refresh a page's position in the queue.
Counting the four cold-start faults is required — memory is initially empty.
cse-1993-ii-c-21.verification: Both simulations re-run step by step; the page-simulator canvas confirms 9 (LRU) and 8 (FIFO) faults.

cse-1993-ii-c-22.approach: Give every edge $S_i\to S_j$ of the precedence graph its own semaphore initialised to 0: $S_i$ does V on it when it finishes, $S_j$ does P on it before it starts. Run one process per statement inside parbegin–parend.

steps.title: Edges
steps.body: From the graph: $S_1\to S_2$ (a), $S_1\to S_3$ (b), $S_2\to S_4$ (c), $S_2\to S_5$ (d), $S_3\to S_5$ (e), $S_6\to S_4$ (f), $S_6\to S_5$ (g) — 7 semaphores, all initially 0.

steps.title: Program
Why it is correct
steps.body: Each P blocks until the matching V has been done, i.e. until the predecessor statement has completed. Every semaphore receives exactly one V and one P, so no process blocks forever and no extra ordering is introduced.

answer.value: Semaphores a–g := 0; parbegin [S1; V(a); V(b)] [P(a); S2; V(c); V(d)] [P(b); S3; V(e)] [P(c); P(f); S4] [P(d); P(e); P(g); S5] [S6; V(f); V(g)] parend

pitfalls: Sharing one semaphore for S5's three predecessors without counting — a single V would release S5 too early.
Forgetting that S6 is an independent source node.
cse-1993-ii-c-22.verification: Checked every edge has one V (at its tail) and one P (at its head); in-degree of S4 = 2 and S5 = 3 match the P counts.

cse-1993-ii-c-23.approach: Join enroll with teach on cno to get the teacher of each enrolled course, filter grade = 'A' and tname = 'Ramesh', join Students for the name, and use DISTINCT since a student may qualify through several courses.

steps.title: Join path
steps.body: Students —(rollno)— enroll —(cno)— teach. (The schema prints `cao` in teach; it is the course number `cno`.)

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT s.rollno, s.sname
FROM   Students s, enroll e, teach t
WHERE  s.rollno = e.rollno
  AND  e.cno    = t.cno
  AND  t.tname  = 'Ramesh'
  AND  e.grade  = 'A';
```

steps.title: Why DISTINCT
steps.body: A student with grade A in two of Ramesh's courses (or a course with two teachers both named Ramesh) would otherwise appear twice; 'at least one' asks for each student once.

answer.value: SELECT DISTINCT s.rollno, s.sname FROM Students s, enroll e, teach t WHERE s.rollno = e.rollno AND e.cno = t.cno AND t.tname = 'Ramesh' AND e.grade = 'A'

pitfalls: Omitting the e.cno = t.cno join gives students with an A in any course whenever Ramesh teaches anything.
cse-1993-ii-c-23.verification: Equivalent nested form: rollno IN (SELECT rollno FROM enroll WHERE grade='A' AND cno IN (SELECT cno FROM teach WHERE tname='Ramesh')).

cse-1993-ii-c-24.approach: Check each relation against its key. teach(tno, tname, cno) has key (tno, cno) but tno → tname depends on part of the key, so it is not even 2NF; split it out.

steps.title: Relations with single-attribute determinants
steps.body: Students: rollno → sname, saddr with key rollno — 3NF (BCNF). courses: cno → cname, key cno — 3NF. enroll: (rollno, cno) → grade, key (rollno, cno) — 3NF. (`sdaddr` in the FD list is a misprint of saddr.)

steps.title: teach violates 3NF
steps.body: teach(tno\*, tname, cno\*) has key (tno, cno), but $$\text{tno}\to\text{tname}$$ is a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of the key. So teach is not in 2NF, hence **the database is not in 3NF**.

steps.title: Normalise
steps.body:
Decompose teach into

- teacher(**tno**, tname)
- teach(**tno, cno**)

The common attribute tno is the key of teacher, so the split is lossless and preserves tno → tname. Final schema: Students(rollno, sname, saddr), courses(cno, cname), enroll(rollno, cno, grade), teacher(tno, tname), teach(tno, cno) — all in 3NF.

answer.value: (a) No. (b) teach(tno, tname, cno) with key (tno, cno) has the partial dependency tno → tname. Decompose into teacher(tno, tname) and teach(tno, cno); the other relations are already in 3NF.

pitfalls: Declaring 3NF because every FD has a key on the left in *some* relation — tname lives in teach, whose key is (tno, cno).
cse-1993-ii-c-24.verification: Closure check: $\{\text{tno},\text{cno}\}^+$ covers teach, but $\{\text{tno}\}^+\ni\text{tname}$ with tno a proper subset of the key.

cse-1993-ii-c-25.approach: One nonterminal S for statements with one production per statement form, and a left-recursive list L of statements separated by ';' for the begin–end block (no EBNF braces or *). Then derive the given statement top-down.

steps.title: Grammar
steps.body: $$\begin{aligned}S &\to \mathbf{id}\ {:=}\ E\\ S &\to \mathbf{for}\ \mathbf{id}\ {:=}\ E\ \mathbf{to}\ E\ \mathbf{do}\ S\\ S &\to \mathbf{begin}\ L\ \mathbf{end}\\ L &\to L\ ;\ S \ \mid\ S\end{aligned}$$ $E$ (expression) is assumed defined; **id** is an identifier token.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body: $S\Rightarrow$ for id := E to E do $S$ (j, 2, 10); inner $S\Rightarrow$ begin $L$ end; $L\Rightarrow L\,;\,S\Rightarrow S\,;\,S$; the two $S$ become x := expr1 and y := expr2.

steps.title: Parse tree
steps.body: Root $S$ uses the for-production; its last child $S$ uses begin $L$ end; $L$ splits as $L\ ;\ S$ with the inner $L\to S$.

answer.value: S → id := E | for id := E to E do S | begin L end;  L → L ; S | S. Parse tree: S(for, j, :=, E(2), to, E(10), do, S(begin, L(L(S(x := expr1)), ;, S(y := expr2)), end)).

pitfalls: Putting ';' after the last statement — the example has none before end, so ';' is a separator, not a terminator.
Using $L\to S\{;S\}$ or $S^*$, which the question forbids.
cse-1993-ii-c-25.verification: Yield of the tree reads: for j := 2 to 10 do begin x := expr1 ; y := expr2 end — exactly the given statement.

cse-1993-ii-c-26.approach: x is a var (call-by-reference) parameter and y is a value parameter. So the caller pushes the address of a and the value of b; inside P, x needs one extra indirection.

steps.title: What is pushed
steps.body: For **var x** the caller pushes the **address (l-value) of a**; for **y** it pushes a **copy of the value (r-value) of b**.

steps.title: Addressing inside P
steps.body: Both live at fixed offsets in P's activation record. **y** is accessed **directly**: its stack slot holds the value, e.g. `M[fp + off_y]`. **x** is accessed **indirectly**: its slot holds a pointer, so every use is `M[M[fp + off_x]]` — and assignments to x change a in the caller.

answer.value: (a) The address of a and the value of b are pushed. (b) y is addressed directly at its stack offset; x is addressed indirectly through the address stored at its offset (one extra level of indirection).

pitfalls: Saying both are pushed by value — the var keyword makes x a reference parameter.
cse-1993-ii-c-26.verification: If P executes x := x + y, the generated code loads M[M[fp+off_x]] and M[fp+off_y] and stores to M[M[fp+off_x]], updating a.

cse-1993-ii-c-27.approach: Track how many consecutive b's end the input so far (0, 1, 2); a third b goes to a trap state. An a always resets the count.

steps.title: States
steps.body: $q_0$: no trailing b (start); $q_1$: one trailing b; $q_2$: two trailing b's; $q_3$: bbb has occurred (dead). $q_0,q_1,q_2$ are accepting.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body: On $b$: $q_0\to q_1\to q_2\to q_3$. On $a$: $q_0,q_1,q_2\to q_0$. $q_3$ loops on $a,b$.

steps.title: Run on bba
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{b}q_1\xrightarrow{b}q_2\xrightarrow{a}q_0$ — the a resets the count; accepted so far.

steps.title: Then bbb
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{b}q_1\xrightarrow{b}q_2\xrightarrow{b}q_3$: three consecutive b's reach the dead state, so **bbabbb is rejected**; prefixes like bbabb are accepted.

answer.value: 4-state DFA: $q_0$ (start), $q_1$, $q_2$ accepting, $q_3$ dead. b: $q_0\to q_1\to q_2\to q_3$; a: $q_0,q_1,q_2\to q_0$; $q_3$ loops on a, b.

pitfalls: Making only $q_0$ accepting — strings ending in b or bb are valid.
Omitting the dead state; a DFA needs a transition on every symbol.
cse-1993-ii-c-27.verification: Minimal: q0, q1, q2 differ by how many more b's are allowed (bb, b, none), and q3 is the only non-accepting state.

cse-1993-ii-c-28.approach: Only associativity is available. Write $q=p*p$ and move brackets for (a); for (b) split on the two possible values of $p*q$.

steps.title: (a) p*q = q*p
steps.body: $$p*q=p*(p*p)=(p*p)*p=q*p$$ using associativity in the middle step.

steps.title: (b) Case p*q = q
steps.body: $$q*q=(p*p)*q=p*(p*q)=p*q=q$$ The set has only two elements, so these are the only cases; in both, $q*q=q$.

answer.value: (a) $p*q=p*(p*p)=(p*p)*p=q*p$. (b) $q*q=(p*p)*q=p*(p*q)$, which is $p*p=q$ if $p*q=p$ and $p*q=q$ if $p*q=q$; so $q*q=q$.

pitfalls: Assuming commutativity — a semigroup need not be commutative; (a) must be derived.
cse-1993-ii-c-28.verification: Model check: the constant semigroup where every product equals q is associative, has p*p = q, and indeed p*q = q*p = q and q*q = q.
